findings.title: sqlExpressions feature flag is ignored because the helper always returns false
findings.body: `enableSqlExpressions` sets `enabled` to the negation of `FlagSqlExpressions` and then returns `false` in both branches. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle therefore has no effect: enabling the documented flag still makes SQL queries fail with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`, and disabling it does the same. If permanent disable is intended, remove or explicitly deprecate the flag and update its documentation; if the flag is supposed to control the feature, this helper must return the flag value. As written the documented toggle is dead and the code hides the intended condition.

findings.title: No regression test verifies SQL expressions are disabled
findings.body: This security fix changes behavior for `QueryTypeSQL`, but no test was added or changed. There is no assertion that a query with `type: sql` is rejected even when `FlagSqlExpressions` is enabled, nor that the disabled path cannot construct or execute an `SQLCommand`. Without such a test, a later change to the helper or the stub DB could silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

findings.title: Stub DB makes SQL command construction fail with a misleading invalid-SQL error
findings.body: `RunCommands` is a stub that always returns an error. `sql.TablesList` calls it, and `NewSQLCommand` calls `TablesList`, so SQL command construction now always fails. Because `NewSQLCommand` converts this into `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", "error reading SQL command")`, users with existing SQL expressions are told their SQL is invalid rather than that SQL expressions have been disabled. The reader path reports a different message. Short-circuit the SQL paths with one consistent disabled-feature error instead of invoking the parser.
